title: rcf define validate reports findings for interface kind, AC class prefix, tacIds and ownerRef or deliveredBy
description: `rcf define validate` (`src/cli/validate.js`) grows four new findings over the walker's existing schema and broken-reference pass: an interface kind outside the closed vocabulary (`INTERFACE_KINDS` in `src/query/gates.js`), a bracketed AC prefix on an AC `description` outside the known classes (`[happy]`, `[edge]`, `[failure]`, `[must-not]`, `[non-functional]`), a `tacIds` naming a non-TAC, and an unresolving `ownerRef` or `deliveredBy`. 0.30.0 PR 8 (DEFINE step 3 spec section 4 validate row, section 11.7 US-17802 appended paragraph): `rcf define validate` reports findings for an interface kind outside the vocabulary, a bracketed AC prefix outside the known classes, a `tacIds` naming a non-TAC, and an unresolving `ownerRef` or `deliveredBy`; absence of a class marker on an AC is NOT a validate finding (that is D4's floor). Each finding exits non-zero (3) alongside the existing schema/broken-reference exit path.
rationale: Spec section 4 pins the validate row's bite: notices on the four categories named here become findings because every legacy and dogfood tree can comply (the vocabularies are closed and small; the resolutions are mechanical). Decision 10 keeps absence of an AC class marker off validate because the dogfood tree and every legacy tree would fail CI on day one: an absence is already D4's finding and D4 is where the ladder for an AC-shape surfaces the gap. Routing bracketed-prefix misuse through validate lets the engineer and the author see the same signal without needing to re-run readiness; the four kinds all share one implementation path (walker already loaded the tree, finding emission is additive).
